Likewise, retained alternative polyA xQTLs were more clearly concentrated toward transcription end sites (gene end) than removed xQTLs.

Colocalizing xQTL and AD GWAS signals

To demonstrate how the xQTLs of six transcriptional modalities of DLPFC could help interpret known AD GWAS signals, we first conducted colocalization analyses leveraging separate-modality xQTL summary data and recent AD GWAS summary data 4 . Assuming a posterior probability colocalization threshold of PP% ' ≥ 0.75, we found that GWAS signals in 54 out of 75 (72%) AD GWAS risk loci 4 colocalized with at least one xQTL signal in the six modalities, with the proportion of colocalized AD GWAS risk loci ranging from 17 (22.7%) to 35 (46.7%) in individual modalities (Table S3, Data S1). Among these 54 colocalized AD risk loci, 37 (68.5%) were colocalized in 2+ modalities (Figure S5), and 19 loci (35.2%) colocalized exclusively with non-expression modalities.

We repeated the colocalization analysis using the cross-modality xQTL summary data to assess the impact of filtering redundant signals arising from correlated RNA traits. Using the same posterior probability colocalization threshold as earlier, we identified 55 colocalized AD GWAS risk loci, of which 24 colocalized to 2+ modalities, consistent with the removal of redundant xQTLs across modalities (Figure 5). Among these 55 loci, 40 were colocalized with expression, while 15 (27.3%) were colocalized exclusively with non-expression modalities and therefore would have been missed by expression-based analyses alone (Table S3, Data S2). These findings demonstrate that non-expression modalities continue to make an important, non-redundant contribution to interpreting AD GWAS signals even after cross-modality refinement of xQTL signals.

Detection and fine mapping of xTWAS risk genes for AD

We next used FUSION (implemented in Pantry) to perform xTWAS that integrated AD GWAS summary data 4 with the multimodal RNA-seq data that we generated from ROS/MAP. For each modality, Table S4 summarizes the number of tested RNA traits, the median cross-validation (CV) R² for the tested RNA traits (i.e., estimate of RNA trait heritability due to cis-SNPs), the number of tested xTWAS genes, and the number of significant xTWAS risk genes. Figure S6 displays respective Manhattan plots of xTWAS results of AD per modality. Applying the Bonferroni-adjusted significance threshold per modality, we identified 214 significant xTWAS genes across all six modalities (Figure S7), including 125 genes that were associated exclusively in non-expression modalities, as well as 58 genes associated with multiple modalities.

To further fine-map independent significant xTWAS genes, we applied the GIFT tool 26 within each local test region (see Methods). We identified 161 independent significant xTWAS genes (Figure 6, Data S3-S8), defined within each modality as those with non-overlapping test genetic regions with any other significant xTWAS genes (Table S5) and those fine-mapped by GIFT (Figure S8-S16). Of these 161 genes, 95 of them were associated exclusively with non-expression modalities, indicating that approximately 59% of detected associations would have been missed in a standard TWAS that considered only expression. Additionally, we note that 48 significant genes possessed signals in multiple modalities, suggesting a shared genetic etiology across multimodal RNA traits.

Independent xTWAS risk genes of AD supported in proteomics data

We considered independent xTWAS risk genes to have proteomic support when their test regions overlapped those of significant PWAS-O risk genes 27 based on DLPFC proteomics data from the same ROS/MAP cohort (see Methods). Among the 161 independent xTWAS risk genes, 64 (39.8%) had genomic regions overlapping genes tested by PWAS-O and could therefore be evaluated at the protein level. Using a PWAS-O significance threshold of q < 0.05, 26 of these 64 genes (40.6%) showed proteomic support across the six modalities (Data S9, Figure S17). Of these 26 genes, 17 (65.4%) were identified exclusively through non-expression modalities, indicating that more than half would have been missed by expressiononly TWAS analyses. For example, ZKSCAN1 was identified exclusively through isoform and alternative polyA modalities. ZKSCAN1, a zinc-finger transcription factor, has been reported to modulate GABA type-A receptors in the brain 47 and was identified as a master dysregulation hub gene whose coexpression networks with other brain regions are rewired in AD 48 . Another example is APOC2, which was identified through isoform, alternative TSS, and alternative polyA modalities. APOC2, which regulates lipid metabolism and cholesterol transport, is located near APOE, a well-known AD risk gene affecting Amyloidβ aggregation and clearance, tau pathology, and neuroinflammation 49, 50 . These observations highlight the value of incorporating non-expression modalities for understanding AD-relevant genetic regulation beyond gene expression. Additionally, six of the 26 genes were supported across multiple modalities. While ZKSCAN1 and APOC2 were identified across multiple non-expression modalities as described above, the remaining four genes (NDUFS2, LACTB, ICA1L, and ENSG00000286923) were supported by both expression and non-expression modalities. In particular, NDUFS2 encodes a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, and LACTB encodes a mitochondrial serine protease that regulates mitochondrial membrane dynamics. Mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are known to play critical roles in the onset and progression of AD 51, 52 , providing a potential link between these genes and AD-related neurodegeneration.

ICA1L is involved in vesicle trafficking and blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, and its downregulation has been associated with vascular leakage, white matter hyperintensities and AD 53 . ENSG00000286923, annotated as the long non-coding RNA ZKSCAN1-1, likely provides cis-regulatory control for the adjacent ZKSCAN1 gene.

PPI network and enrichment analyses of independent xTWAS risk genes of AD

Using the STRING webtool, we performed PPI network analyses using 161 independent xTWAS risk genes in all six modalities (Figure 7A), for illustrating shared biological processes. PPI edges represent predicted functional associations and were colored according to different data sources, including co-expression, experimental data, curated databases, gene fusion, co-occurrence, neighborhood, and text mining. Of the 161 genes, 107 were represented in the STRING network, of which 75 genes (46.6%) formed interconnected PPI networks (PPI enrichment p-value < 1.0 × 10 ! $( ). This integrated network contained clusters centered around well-established AD risk genes, including MAPT, PICALM, APOC2, BIN1, TREM2, ABCA7, CRHR1, and ACE. These findings support that multimodal transcriptional traits share . biological networks, and that gene regulations affect AD genetic risk factors through multiple transcriptional mechanisms.

Additionally, pathway enrichment analysis using all 161 independent xTWAS risk genes showed significant enrichment in several AD-relevant biological pathways (Figure 7B). We observed the strongest enrichment for T cell activation (FDR q-value 1.21 × 10 !" ), a pathway implicated in AD pathogenesis through its contribution to neuroinflammation 54 , with leading risk genes of BIN1, BLNK, EGFR, INPP5D, and MAPT. Particularly, INPP5D encodes SHIP1, a negative regulator of immune signaling that has been implicated in AD through its role in microglial inflammasome activation, autophagy dysregulation, and neuroinflammation 55 . We observed additional significant enrichment for Toll receptor signaling pathway activation (FDR q-value 0.0169), with leading risk genes PPP4C, EGFR, NECTIN2, and MICA; B cell activation (FDR q-value 0.0408) with leading risk genes EGFR, BLNK, INPP5D, MAPT, and BIN1; and inflammation mediated by chemokine and cytokine signaling (FDR q-value 0.0397), with leading risk genes EGFR, BLNK, ITGA2B, and PHKG2). Together, these results further highlight the importance of immune and neuroinflammatory processes in AD pathogenesis.

Beyond immune-related pathways, we note that we observed enrichment of several cellular signaling pathways, including integrin signaling (FDR q-value 0.0076), with leading risk genes EGFR, ITGA2B, ITGAX, and PLD2; and axon guidance mediated by semaphorins (FDR q-value 0.0334), with leading risk genes PLD2, ARHGAP45, and MAPT. Axon guidance has been implicated in AD pathogenesis through the regulation of hallmark proteins, including amyloid-β and tau hyperphosphorylation 56 , while integrin signaling contributes to neuroinflammation, BBB dysfunction, and Amyloid-β toxicity 57 . Additional enriched pathways included blood coagulation (FDR q-value 0.0388) with leading risk genes C4BPB, INPP5D, and ITGA2B, and heme biosynthesis (FDR q-value 0.0417), involving EARS2, PPOX.

We also examined PPI networks of independent xTWAS risk genes within each individual transcriptional modality (Figure S18). Across modalities, 20.7% to 52.4% of independent xTWAS risk genes formed interconnected networks and several well-established AD risk genes -including MAPT, PICALM, CRHR1, APOC2, and KANSL1 -recurred as hub genes across multiple RNA regulatory modalities. In the expression, isoform ratio, and alternative TSS modalities, 30.3% (20 out of 66), 34.6% (18 out of 53), and 30% (12 out of 40) of genes formed connected PPI networks, respectively, centered on known AD risk genes such as MAPT and PICALM. In RNA stability, splice junction, and alternative polyA modalities, 52.4% (11 out of 21), 20.7% (6 out of 29), and 28.6% (12 out of 42) genes were interconnected in PPI networks, respectively, centered on genes such as CRHR1 and KANSL1. These findings show that distinct RNA regulatory modalities capture partially different interaction networks while converging on a shared set of AD-related hub genes and biological pathways.

Discussion

This study shows that multimodal RNA phenotyping of postmortem DLPFC tissue can substantially expand AD risk-gene discovery beyond expression-only approaches. Using ROS/MAP RNA-seq data, we profiled six transcriptomic modalities, performed xQTL mapping, colocalized regulatory signals with AD GWAS loci, and conducted xTWAS analyses to identify genes whose genetically regulated RNA traits were associated with AD risk. The key findings across all six transcriptomic modalities are summarized in Figure S19. Nearly 30% of xGenes (~7,500 genes) from separate-modality mapping were detected exclusively through non-expression modalities, and cross-modality mapping refined these signals by reducing redundant xQTLs while preserving biologically interpretable modality-specific patterns, consistent with previous findings from the Pantry study 20 . Cross-modality xQTLs colocalized with 55 of 75 reported AD GWAS risk loci, including 15 loci showing colocalization exclusively with non-expression modalities, underscoring the complementary value of multimodal RNA traits for interpreting AD genetic risk.

By integrating ROS/MAP multimodal transcriptomic data with GWAS summary statistics of Alzheimer's disease 4 , we identified 213 significant xTWAS genes across six modalities, which were subsequently finemapped to 161 independent xTWAS risk genes. Following xTWAS fine mapping, the relative distribution of significant genes across modalities remained highly consistent with the initial xTWAS results, supporting robust contribution of each individual modality (Figure S20). Notably, 59% of these independent xTWAS risk genes were only detected in non-expression modalities, and nearly 30% of fine-mapped independent xTWAS risk genes were detected in multiple modalities. These findings demonstrate that incorporating regulatory modalities beyond gene expression substantially improves detection of xTWAS findings for AD dementia. We further obtained proteomic support for 26 independent xTWAS risk genes using PWAS-O results derived from DLPFC proteomic data from ROS/MAP; 17 (65.4%) of which would have been missed if we had only considered gene expression in TWAS analyses. Six of these proteomically supported genes were supported by multiple transcriptional modalities, including genes involved in mitochondrial dysfunction and bioenergetic failure (NDUFS2, LACTB), lipoprotein metabolism and neuroinflammation (APOC2), and blood-brain barrier integrity (ICA1L).

Using the STRING tool, we found that 20%-52% of independent xTWAS risk genes formed interaction networks within individual modalities. Integrating independent xTWAS risk genes across all six modalities further expanded functional connectivity, with approximately 47% of genes forming interaction networks centered around established AD risk genes such as MAPT, PICALM, APOC2, BIN1, TREM2, ABCA7, CRHR1 and ACE. Studies have previously implicated these hub genes influencing AD through diverse biological mechanisms. MAPT encodes the tau protein, a key neuropathological biomarker of AD pathology 58 , and PICALM, which encodes a clathrin assembly protein and has been implicated in AD pathogenesis through the regulation of amyloid-β (Ac) production, transport, and clearance, as well as tauopathy and synaptic dysfunction 59 . BIN1(Bridging Integrator 1), one of the strongest genetic risk factors for AD, has been associated with proinflammatory responses, modulation of synaptic activity, and diseaseassociated microglial pathway 60, 61 . TREM2 has been implicated in AD through its roles in microglial metabolism, phagocytosis, and interaction with APOE 62 . ABCA7 dysfunction is associated with increased Aβ production, reduced Aβ clearance, impaired microglia response to inflammation, and endoplasmic reticulum stress 63 . CRHR1, which encodes a G-protein-coupled receptor that binds corticotropin-releasing hormone family neuropeptides, has also been implicated in AD through Aβ production and stress-related neuronal dysfunction 64.

Consistent with the PPI network results, independent xTWAS risk genes were significantly enriched in ADrelevant immune, neuroinflammatory, and cellular signaling pathways. Several enrichments were observed primarily among genes identified through non-expression modalities. For example, integrin signalling was significantly enriched among genes identified through alternative TSS usage and isoform ratio modalities, whereas axon guidance mediated by semaphorins was significantly enriched in the alternative TSS modality (Figure S21). These pathways were not significantly enriched in the expression modality alone, highlighting that non-expression RNA traits capture complementary biological mechanisms relevant to AD. Altogether, these results demonstrate the importance of studying multimodal transcriptional traits to fully leverage the information embedded within RNA-seq data.

Nonetheless, several limitations should be considered when interpreting our findings. First, xTWAS and xQTL analyses remain inferential and cannot establish that prioritized genes or regulatory modalities causally influence AD risk; associations may reflect LD, shared cis-regulatory architecture, correlated nearby genes, or polygenicity in GWAS summary statistics [65] [66] [67] . To reduce false-positive inflation, we applied conservative Bonferroni correction to account for multiple testing and used GIFT to fine map xTWAS associations and identify independent xTWAS risk genes. Second, our analyses were restricted to cis-SNPs within a ±500 kb window around each gene TSS. Although this cis-window is commonly used in TWAS studies, trans-regulatory effects account for a substantial proportion of RNA-trait heritability 68, 69

Additional limitations relate to sample context and generalizability. The transcriptomic and proteomic analyses were conducted in bulk postmortem DLPFC tissue from European-ancestry ROS/MAP participants, which may obscure cell-type-specific regulation and limit generalizability across brain regions, disease stages, ancestries, and living-state biology. Proteomic follow-up was limited to a subset of xTWAS genes that could be evaluated using PWAS-O results based on DLPFC data from the same ROS/MAP cohort, so independent replication in diverse cohorts, additional brain regions, and cell-type-resolved datasets will be important. In summary, this multimodal transcriptomic framework identified AD-associated genes that would likely be missed by expression-only TWAS approaches, demonstrating that AD genetic risk may act through multiple layers of transcriptional regulation. Genes supported across multiple RNA modalities may represent particularly compelling candidates because convergent regulatory signals may reflect more robust biological involvement in disease pathogenesis. These findings support integrating diverse transcriptomic traits to better capture the complexity of AD genetic regulation and motivate future multimodal analyses across additional tissues, cell types, ancestries, and disease stages. This study included 64,498 clinically diagnosed AD cases, 46,828 proxy AD and related dementia (proxy-ADD), and 677,663 controls. We note that the variants in the APOE gene region were capped by their GWAS p-values<1e-300 in this public GWAS summary data which limited the representation of extremely significant variants in APOE locus, including the well-established AD risk variants APOE E2 (rs7412) and APOE E4 (rs429358). In this study, we were only able to consider 16 variants in the APOE region 19:44905791-44909393, including two genome-wide significant variants rs769448 (19: 44906322; GWAS p-value = 7.81E-14) and rs769452 (19: 44907853; GWAS p-value = 7.49E-18).

R package. We first implemented the Sum of Single Conditions (SuSiE) framework 36 to map independent xQTL and GWAS signals per locus defined as ±500 kb around the GWAS lead signal. Reference linkage disequilibrium (LD r 2 ) was calculated by PLINK2(v2.00a4.3) 37 using the ROS/MAP WGS data. Second, we computed posterior probabilities for each pair of fine-mapped xQTL or GWAS signals with respect to five hypotheses: no association with the corresponding transcriptomic trait and AD (% # ), association with AD only (% $ ), association with transcriptomic trait only (% % ), association with both transcriptomic trait and AD but distinct causal variants (% & ), and association with both transcriptomic trait and AD through a shared "causal" variant (% ' ). We used posterior probability of % ' greater than 0.75 (PP% ' ≥ 0.75) to claim colocalization of the test xQTL and GWAS signal.

, and incorporating both cis-and trans-xQTLs into future TWAS frameworks may improve risk-gene discovery. Third, the genetically regulated components of multiple RNA traits per gene may exhibit heterogeneous genetic effect directions. Although ACAT efficiently aggregates trait-level TWAS p-values into gene-level p-value per gene, it does not incorporate effect size direction, so future methods that jointly model multiple RNA traits per gene may further improve interpretation and power. Analysis scripts used in this study are available from https://github.com/krkim1822/AD-multimodaltranscriptomics. Cis-xQTLs, Colocalization results, xTWAS model weights, and xTWAS summary data are available from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21923545.

Figure 2. Characteristics of mapped xQTL of six transcriptional modalities by separate-modality analyses. (A) Number of unique xGenes per modality, colored by the count of independent xQTLs. (B) Histogram of the number of xGenes according to the number of their independent xQTL signals, summed over all six modalities. (C) Modality proportions of xQTLs among xQTL signals per within-xGene rank. TensorQTL assigns rank to independent QTLs for each xGene in order of their detections by stepwise regression. Rank 1 captures the top primary signal per xGene, with subsequent ranks representing conditionally independent effects of decreasing strength. The number above the bars indicate the number of independent xQTLs per rank.
